claim: Martin uses almost only native English prefixes (un-, be-) and the archaic positional prefix a- (atop, abed, ahorse), while Latin and Greek prefixes are largely absent.

verdict.note: Exact sentence follows the list of Latin/Greek prefixes ('Their absence speaks volumes'). Page then states Martin 'uses almost exclusively English (i.e. Anglo-Saxon) prefixes', gives un-/be- examples, and names 'the archaic prefix a- to denote position: atop, abed, ahorse'. claim: Martin favours Old English suffixes such as -craft, -dom, -ness, -hood and -less to lend historical depth.

verdict.trueWording: convey a deep sense of their Anglo-Saxon provenance
verdict.note: Exact phrase: 'Martin overwhelmingly uses forms which convey a deep sense of their Anglo-Saxon provenance.' All five suffixes named in the claim (-craft, -dom, -ness, -hood, -less) appear in the page's list, each glossed with an Old English etymology; the page adds these 'convey a richness and historical depth'.

claim: Martin builds an otherworld texture from Anglo-Saxon-style compounds (longsword, godswood, oathbreaker, weirwood) and coins many new ones (sellsword, dragonglass, greenseer, smallfolk, skinchanger).

verdict.trueWording: coin scores of wonderful and evocative neologisms
verdict.note: Page reads 'Martin uses this facility to coin scores of wonderful and evocative neologisms' — the quote inflects 'coin' as 'coins', so not word for word. Substance fully supported: longsword and oathbreaker appear in the compound-word list; godswood, weirwood, sellsword, dragonglass, greenseer, smallfolk and skinchanger all appear in the neologism list, and the page ties them to 'the otherness of his fantasy world'.

claim: Rare neoclassical words (fornication, adultery, intercession) are reserved for learned or legal speakers and contexts, standing out against the Saxon backdrop.

verdict.trueWording: technocratic and legalistic mindset of medieval religious inquisitors
verdict.note: Page has the two adjectives in the reverse order from the quote, so not verbatim. Substance holds: 'intercession' is spoken by Maester Colemon, 'a learned man, and so it is in character'; 'fornication' and 'adultery' occur in the High Septon's religious court; and the page says that 'against the overwhelming backdrop of Saxon vocabulary... the rare use of technocratic neoclassical combining words is very conspicuous'.

claim: Martin consistently chooses Anglo-Saxon-origin words and generally avoids Latinate and neoclassical vocabulary.

claim: Mannerisms such as 'oft', 'elsewise' and dropping -ly ('like to be') are criticised as irritating pseudo-archaism.

verdict.trueWording: would-be medievalisms which become annoying mannerisms

The page lists exactly the three mannerisms claimed: 'The most persistent one is removing the -ly suffix from adverbs. He is like to be angry'; 'Oft instead of the sensible often'; 'Elsewise'. claim: Martin says he has always written in tight third person because that is how people perceive events.

verdict.trueWording: I've always written from a tight third-person point of view
verdict.note: Exact phrase in Martin's own answer, and the reason follows immediately: 'because I think that's the way we perceive things. None of us are omniscient.' Byline 'Amy Gentry' and the 2013 date are confirmed on the page, so the attribution is accurate.

claim: Martin rejects omniscient narration on the grounds that no one is omniscient and we only hear our own thoughts.
quote: None of us are omniscient.

verdict.trueWording: None of us are omniscient.
verdict.note: Exact. Martin: "I've always written from a tight third-person point of view, because I think that's the way we perceive things. None of us are omniscient... the only thoughts we hear are our own thoughts." Both halves of the claim (no one is omniscient; we only hear our own thoughts) are on the page in Martin's own words.

claim: Switching POV characters costs Martin days of work to recover that character's voice.
quote: struggle for a few days trying to get back the voice

verdict.trueWording: struggle for a few days trying to get back the voice
verdict.note: Exact. Full sentence: "When I do make that transition from one character to another, I usually struggle for a few days trying to get back the voice of the character I'm just returning to after some hiatus." Supports the claim precisely.

claim: Martin checks every sentence against what the focal character could actually understand at that moment.
quote: does he understand what's happening?

verdict.trueWording: does he understand what's happening?
verdict.note: Exact (page uses a curly apostrophe). Full: "You have to really look at every sentence and say, okay, he's in the middle of this, does he understand what's happening? What words would he think?" Caveat: Martin says this specifically about Bran, the youngest POV character, as the reason those chapters are hardest to write; the claim generalises it to every focal character. Sentence-level epistemic filtering is genuinely described, but the page anchors it to writing a 7-or-8-year-old.

claim: Martin writes chapters out of reading order, staying in one character's voice.
quote: I don't write the chapters in the order

verdict.trueWording: I don't write the chapters in the order
verdict.note: Exact. Full: "Well, I don't write the chapters in the order in which you read them. I get into a character's voice." The staying-in-one-voice half is also supported: "I tend to write not just one chapter by that character, but three or four."

claim: Martin alternates battle writing between a soldier's close-up viewpoint and a general's distant overview.
source: Bernard Cornwell, 'Interview with George R. R. Martin'
quote: Sometimes I employ the private's viewpoint

verdict.trueWording: Sometimes I employ the private's viewpoint
verdict.note: Exact. From Martin's question to Cornwell, so genuinely his own words: "Sometimes I employ the private's viewpoint, very up close and personal... Sometimes I go with the general's point of view instead, looking down from on high, seeing lines and flanks and reserves." The alternation claim is fully supported.

claim: Martin defends dense food, heraldry and sound description as vicarious experience meant to be tasted, seen and heard.
source: ComicBook.com on Martin's Official Game of Thrones Cookbook foreword, 2024
quote: I want them to taste the food.

verdict.trueWording: I want them to taste the food.
verdict.note: Quote exact on the ComicBook page. Food, heraldry ("seven golden hedgehogs on a field of dark green") and "Fiction gives us vicarious experience" are all present. However, the claim's sound/hearing element is NOT on this page — ComicBook truncates the foreword and contains no reference to hearing or the clash of steel. That fuller passage ("I want them to see the colors of the knights' surcoats... I want them to hear the clash of steel on steel") appears on the Winter Is Coming page (claim 21's URL), not this one. The 'seen and heard' portion of the claim is unsupported by the cited source.

verdict.note: Exact. Both halves supported on the page: "'gratuitous' usually translates to 'more than I wanted' or 'did not advance the plot'" and "Nothing is gratuitous, as I see it. It is all part of the experience."

Context supports the claim's contrast: the architect "lays out the blueprints... every detail of the house is worked out before a single nail is drawn," while gardeners "dig a hole and they plant a seed and they see what comes up."

claim: Significant deaths follow a memoryless geometric distribution in chapter (discourse) order but a power law in story time, producing felt unpredictability.
quote: well described by a geometric distribution

verdict.trueWording: well described by a geometric distribution
verdict.note: Both halves confirmed, not inferred. Discourse time: interevent times "are well described by a geometric distribution and are therefore memoryless." Story time: memorylessness "can be rejected" and deaths are "well described by a power-law distribution with a lower cutoff" (alpha approx. 2.00). The paper states the contrast directly: "it is geometric rather than power law." Unpredictability is claimed as "measurable support" for deaths being "unpredictable chapter by chapter."

claim: Martin decouples plot sequence from chronology as a defamiliarizing device to engage readers.

verdict.trueWording: defamiliarization ... a device for engaging the reader in the story
verdict.note: No quotation was supplied, so VERBATIM is not applicable. Substance is fully supported: the paper credits Schklovsky with emphasizing "defamiliarization (decoupling the temporal sequence of the plot from the chronological storyline) as a device for engaging the reader in the story," then adds "Our analysis of significant deaths highlights how effectively Martin exploits this technique." Attribution nuance: the concept is Schklovsky's; the authors credit Martin with exploiting it.

claim: Chapters are third-person narration heavily focalized with free indirect discourse, so villains become sympathetic in their own POV.

Post dated Mar 5, 2011, matching the cited year.

For instance, members of House Lannister often refer to Varys as the 'Spider' in conversation, and Tyrion constantly jokes with Varys about being a eunuch." Both traits ('the Spider', eunuch) named. Byline Gavin Hurley, published Sep 25, 2019, matching the citation.

claim: World description unfolds with fluid lyricism without Tolkien-style descriptive tedium.
quote: without ever lapsing into Tolkienesque descriptive tedium

verdict.trueWording: without ever lapsing into Tolkienesque descriptive tedium
verdict.note: Full sentence carries the claim's other half verbatim too: "Accounts of the mythic world unfold with fluid lyricism, without ever lapsing into Tolkienesque descriptive tedium (yes, I know that's heresy)." Page is 'Literature Commentary: A Song of Ice and Fire (Books 1-3)', dated 07 Jun, on literaryanalysis.net.

verdict.trueWording: give each character their own unique voice

claim: Carroll reads the series as 'Barbaric Age' medievalism that foregrounds visceral violence as a narrative strategy rather than subtle prose technique.

verdict.trueWording: virile, brute force

Violence emphasis confirmed: "violent, dark, brutal, and relentlessly masculine" and "hyper-violence." TWO CAVEATS: (1) 'virile, brute force' is Umberto Eco's phrase (1986, 'Dreaming of the Middle Ages') that Carroll quotes, not Carroll's own wording; (2) the claim's trailing contrast 'rather than subtle prose technique' is absent from the source — the word 'prose' appears zero times and the article never contrasts violence with prose technique. That clause is the claim-writer's framing, unsupported though not contradicted.

Individual chapters are told from the point of view of the character after whom they are named." The supplied quote appears word for word, and the surrounding sentence supports both halves of the claim (titled with, and narrated from, the POV character). feature: Scholarly coverage of language and narration

source: McFarland, Mastering the Game of Thrones (Battis & Johnston eds.), 2015

verdict.trueWording: Section "Language and Narration": Peterson, Napolitano, Cowlishaw
verdict.note: Table of contents lists, under the section heading "Language and Narration": "The Languages of Ice and Fire (David J. Peterson) 15", "'Sing for your little life': Story, Discourse and Character (Marc Napolitano) 35", "What Maesters Knew: Narrating Knowing (Brian Cowlishaw) 57". Page also confirms "Copyright Date: 2015" and "Edited by Jes Battis and Susan Johnston". Every element of the claim holds. One paraphrase to flag: Peterson's essay is titled "The Languages of Ice and Fire", not "invented languages" — the page never uses the word "invented", though the blurb does cite "the origins of the Dothraki language", so the gloss is fair rather than sourced.

claim: Martin's vocabulary systematically excludes almost all Latin-, Greek- and French-derived words in favour of native Old English roots.

verdict.trueWording: systematic exclusion of almost all words derived from Latin, Greek, French
verdict.note: Abstract: "distinguished ... by a systematic exclusion from his vocabulary of almost all words derived from Latin, Greek, French or other languages", followed by "Instead, his style shows a high frequency of words of Anglo-Saxon origin." The conclusion restates it: "Latinate words or affixes ... are mostly excluded." Claim tracks the source closely. Two caveats on the source rather than the claim: it is a personal blog (by "Simon"), and the author's own count is internally inconsistent — mid-post he cites "intermittent" as the standout Latinate word in A Feast for Crows, while the conclusion says he noticed "only one really Latinate word, 'intermediate'".

claim: The medieval texture rests on dense two-root native compounds (battleground, bedchamber, breastplate, drawbridge, longship, warhammer) and coinages cast in the same mould (weirwood, greensight, skinchanger, ironborn, sellsword, shadowcat, godswood, greenseer).

verdict.trueWording: overwhelming tendency to use Anglo-Saxon source words to form compound words
verdict.note: All fourteen cited words verified individually in the raw text. The six compounds (battleground, bedchamber, breastplate, drawbridge, longship, warhammer) all appear in the post's alphabetical list of compounds found in A Feast for Crows; the eight coinages (weirwood, greensight, skinchanger, ironborn, sellsword, shadowcat, godswood, greenseer) all appear in its list of neologisms, and the post separately singles out "weirwood, greensight, skinchanger" as "genuinely visionary and inspired". Supporting wording: compounds "show an overwhelming tendency to use Anglo-Saxon or archaic source words ... to describe mostly medieval, warlike or feudal concepts". Minor framing note: "two-root" comes from the post's general definition of English compounds ("tend to combine two short, often monosyllabic, words"), not from a statement made specifically about Martin.

claim: Martin uses native prefixes (un-, be-) and Old English suffixes (-craft, -dom, -hood, -ness, -ship, -some, -ward) while Latinate prefixes such as sub- and super- are almost absent.

verdict.trueWording: Martin uses almost exclusively English (i.e. Anglo-Saxon) prefixes
verdict.note: Prefixes: "Instead, Martin uses almost exclusively English (i.e. Anglo-Saxon) prefixes. Common examples are 'un-' and 'be-' forms." Latinate absence: "There are hardly if any words starting ab, sub, super, post… Their absence speaks volumes" — sub- and super- named explicitly, matching the claim. All seven suffixes are present in the post's list and each is explicitly sourced to Old English: -craft, -dom, -hood, -ness, -ship, -some, -ward(s). (-hood renders as "– hood" with an en dash in the extracted text, which is why a naive grep for "-hood" misses it; it is present at line 69 as "– hood (from the Old English -hād)".)

claim: Latinate and neoclassical words are reserved for legal, religious, courtly or maester speech, so a learned or technocratic register stands out against the native default.

verdict.trueWording: deployed for effect in the context of legal or religious or courtly matters
verdict.note: Conclusion: Latinate words "are mostly excluded or only deployed for effect in the context of legal or religious or courtly matters". The maester element is explicit: "Maester Colemon says 'intercession' ... but then, he is a maester, a learnèd man, and so it is in character", plus a final chapter "about the educated maesters of Oldtown" carrying "penetrate", "complement", "complaint". The technocratic/standing-out element is also explicit: "fornication" is "deployed to convey technocratic and legalistic mindset of medieval religious inquisitors", and "the rare use of technocratic neoclassical combining words is very conspicuous". All four register contexts named in the claim (legal, religious, courtly, maester) are on the page.

claim: The prose swings between functional modern-thriller register and prose larded with faux-medievalisms, sometimes on a single page.

verdict.trueWording: veers from functional modern thriller prose to prose larded with fake medievalisms
verdict.note: Opening paragraph: Martin's style "is unstable. By this I mean it veers from purely functional modern thriller prose to prose larded with fake medievalisms". The single-page element is the next sentence: "On the same page there can be 'ofts' and 'elsewises' from the 15th century and then things being 'divvied up'". The claim's "faux-medievalisms" is a synonym for the page's "fake medievalisms"; everything else matches, including the thriller framing.

claim: Martin's baseline style is lucid, functional and clear despite the fantasy setting.

verdict.trueWording: The default setting of Martin's style is lucid and functional
verdict.note: Section 1, headed "Crisp": "The default setting of Martin's style is lucid and functional." "Clear" is supported by the conclusion's reference to his "otherwise swift clear style". The "despite the fantasy setting" clause is supported by: "There are a few nods in the direction of cod-medievalism, a few stylistic gestures towards the books' fantasy setting ... But these tics don't conceal the fundamental modernity of the prose."

claim: Archaism is manufactured by dropping the -ly from adverbs and using forms like 'oft', 'elsewise' and 'like to be'.

verdict.trueWording: The most persistent one is removing the -ly suffix from adverbs
verdict.note: Section 9 ("Cod medievalism") lists as mannerisms: "The most persistent one is removing the -ly suffix from adverbs. 'He is like to be angry'; 'He has near finished the task.'", then "'Oft' instead of the sensible 'often'" and "'Elsewise'". All three cited forms are on the page. Small structural nuance: 'like to be' is given as an instance of the -ly dropping (like/likely) rather than as a separate archaism alongside oft and elsewise, but the claim's grouping does not distort the source.

claim: Fifteenth-century archaisms sit beside modern New York colloquialisms ('divvied up', 'what's that all about') on the same page.

verdict.trueWording: 'ofts' and 'elsewises' from the 15th century ... as if in modern New York
verdict.note: Opening paragraph, verbatim: "On the same page there can be 'ofts' and 'elsewises' from the 15th century and then things being 'divvied up' or people asking 'What's that all about?' as if in modern New York." Both embedded fragments were confirmed present in the raw text: "divvied up" exactly, and "What's that all about?" differing from the claim only in capitalisation and terminal question mark. Graded SUBSTANCE rather than VERBATIM only because the claim record carries no designated quote field.

claim: Outside violence, the plain style can achieve a powerfully simple beauty.

verdict.trueWording: GRRM's limpid style can have a powerfully simple beauty
verdict.note: Section 2 ("Poetry"): "When his characters are not swearing or chopping off each others' heads, GRRM's limpid style can have a powerfully simple beauty." The phrase "powerfully simple beauty" was confirmed verbatim in the raw text, and the "outside violence" condition is exactly the source's "not swearing or chopping off each others' heads" clause. The post attaches the observation to Arya Stark's Braavos chapters.

claim: Words such as 'cool' and 'still' recur within a single passage, read either as atmospheric effect or as haste.

verdict.trueWording: repetitions of 'cool' and 'still' — signs of haste, or careful repetitions
verdict.note: Parenthetical following the Water Palace passage: "(I can't decide whether the repetitions in this passage – of 'cool' and 'still' – are signs of haste, or careful repetitions designed to evoke the lazy, torpid atmosphere of Lord Martell's sea retreat.)" Both words, the single-passage scope, and the two competing readings (atmosphere vs haste) are all present. The claim's neutral "read either as" correctly preserves the author's stated undecidedness rather than picking a side.

claim: Confrontations are carried by terse, charged dialogue whose implications land as shock.

verdict.trueWording: Confrontations between opposing characters are done though terse, charged dialogue
verdict.note: Section 4 ("Dramatic dialogue"): "Confrontations between opposing characters are done though terse, charged dialogue. As a reader on numerous occasions you experience a real dramatic shock when you realise, along with one character, the implications of another one's words, and are horrified or shocked." Both halves of the claim — terse charged dialogue, and implications landing as shock — are explicit. ("though" is the source's own typo for "through"; quoted as it stands.)

claim: Martin coins new medieval-sounding words (septon, maester, warg) and scores of compound neologisms (sellsword, smallfolk, godswood, greenseer).

verdict.trueWording: coined completely new, medieval-sounding words; coin scores of neologisms
verdict.note: Section 6: "Martin has coined completely new, medieval-sounding words to fit the fantasy medievalism of the story ... Sept and septon and septa ..., maester (doctor/alchemist), ... warg (human who can inhabit an animal)". Section 7: "Martin uses this facility to coin scores of neologisms: sellsword (mercenary), smallfolk (ordinary people) ... godswood ... greenseer". All seven cited words confirmed in the raw text, and the claim's split between the two categories matches the post's own two-section division. Unrelated to the claim, but the post's coinage list is loose in one spot: it includes "pyromancer", a pre-existing Greek-derived English word.

claim: Ordinary words are slightly deformed into strange forms by repetition ('Ser' for Sir, 'flowered' for menstruation).

verdict.trueWording: slight deformation of existing standard words into something rich and strange
verdict.note: Section 5 ("Distorting English"): "Martin employs the slight deformation of existing standard words or phrases into something rich and strange. A frequent example is that knights ... are called 'Ser', an obvious distortion of the traditional Sir, which starts out sounding silly but, by sheer repetition, comes to seem the natural term. Similarly, girls who have had their first period have 'flowered'." Both examples confirmed verbatim in the raw text, and the repetition mechanism the claim cites is the source's own ("by sheer repetition", "By repetition over the multiple scenes"). The claim's "for menstruation" is a fair gloss of "girls who have had their first period".

claim: Words meant to sound medieval are overused to the point of pretension, 'jape' replacing joke every time.

verdict.trueWording: uses the word "jape" instead of joke… "aside from its pretentiousness"
verdict.note: Page: "Whenever he talks about someone joking around, he uses the word 'jape' instead of joke. Jape, aside from its pretentiousness, is a singularly displeasing word." The overuse framing is also supported: "Martin leans on words that I presume he thinks sound archaic and exotic. In reality they just sound ridiculous." Minor wording drift: the essay says "archaic and exotic", not "medieval" (though "faux-medieval flourishes" appears earlier in the same post). "jape" and "pretentiousness" are verbatim; the claim sentence as a whole is a paraphrase.

claim: A single phrase, 'mummer's farce', is applied to nearly every council and hostile meeting, dozens of times per book.

verdict.trueWording: "the phrase comes up at least ten times in every book"
verdict.note: FREQUENCY IS INFLATED — fix before use. Page: "Do you really need to describe every king's council and meeting between frenemies as a 'mummer's farce'? Seriously, the phrase comes up at least ten times in every book." The essay says AT LEAST TEN times per book, not "dozens". The "nearly every council and hostile meeting" half is well supported ("every king's council and meeting between frenemies"). Note: a higher count ("at least a hundred instances", "every half dozen pages") appears only in reader comments below the post, not in Gelzer-Govatos's text, so it cannot back "dozens" under this attribution.

claim: The prose is otherwise serviceable, but the faux-medieval flourishes periodically overreach.

verdict.trueWording: "prose borders on the servicable… faux-medieval flourishes go a bridge too far"
verdict.note: Closest of the fifteen to verbatim. Page: "Most of the time his prose borders on the servicable, but there are times when his faux-medieval flourishes go a bridge too far." ("servicable" is the author's own misspelling.) "faux-medieval flourishes" is verbatim; "borders on the servicable" is slightly weaker than the claim's flat "is serviceable", and the essay says "most of the time", not "otherwise".

claim: Some characters are voiced through a compulsively repeated phrase (Hodor's name; Reek's rhyme with a swapped last word).

verdict.trueWording: "Annoying Speech Mannerisms"; Hodor "can only say his own name"
verdict.note: Page section heading "Annoying Speech Mannerisms": "Martin frequently employs particular speech patters [sic]". Hodor is "a mentally handicapped stable boy who can only say his own name, Hodor". Reek: "he repeats a rhyme to remember who he is… Reek, my name is Reek, it rhymes with [random word that rhymes with Reek]", with "slight variations" (weak, squeak) — exactly the claim's "rhyme with a swapped last word". Both examples confirmed.

claim: Sex scenes drop into clichéd, overwrought language disconnected from the surrounding register.

verdict.trueWording: "the scenes themselves are clunky to the extreme"… elsewhere adequate, here "he dips"
verdict.note: Page: "the scenes themselves are clunky to the extreme. They usually involve someone being drunk with desire for the other person, their head swimming with the wine of lust or some such nonsense" — supports "clichéd, overwrought". The register break is explicit: "If in most other areas Martin's prose acheives a level of adequatulence, in his sex scenes he dips to what I imagine is the level of writing found in those books… with titles like The Incredible Hunk". The essay's own vocabulary is "clunky"/"dire"/"slimy", not "disconnected from the surrounding register".

claim: Martin attaches fixed epithets and formulaic tags to people and things in the manner of Homeric oral formula.

verdict.trueWording: "the real Martinian stock phrases are those faces still as masks"
verdict.note: The essay is titled "George R.R. Martin, The American Homer", subtitled "The Influence of the Oral Tradition". It defines the term the claim uses: "Homer… is well known for the use of epithets, stock phrases that attend a character or concept. Dawn is always rosy-fingered; Athena is grey-eyed", then applies it — "I now think of Martin as one of those minstrels" — and lists Martin's tags: faces "still as masks", "dark with anger", men "corded or thick with muscle", maidens "whose hair shines like spun gold". Fully supported; the word "epithets" is the essay's own.

claim: Stock phrases give the writer and reader breathing room, like a minstrel's filler lines.

verdict.trueWording: stock phrases "give their audience time to absorb"; for a writer, momentum
verdict.note: Both halves are on the page but from two places. Reader breathing room comes from the NYT block quote the essay adopts: minstrels "fell back on such stock phrases to give their audience time to absorb what had just been sung and to give themselves a moment to think about what they were going to sing next." The writer half is the essayist's own: "for a writer, they come easily off the pen. Very important for maintaining momentum… stock phrases are thermals", and "it's functioning as a literary ummm, as with those minstrels". The minstrel analogy is explicit and central.

claim: No single sentence carries much force; the effect is cumulative across the run of prose rather than sentence-level.

verdict.trueWording: "no single sentence is that effective, but a full cartridge"
verdict.note: Page: "Martin keeps us turning pages with a steady flow of low-density sentences. It's shotgun writing: like buckshot, no single sentence is that effective, but a full cartridge of it gets the point across." "low-density sentences" is verbatim and matches the claim's feature label exactly. Cumulative-not-sentence-level is precisely the buckshot figure.

claim: Recurring stock similes such as 'black as night' work as visual shorthand that relies on reader familiarity rather than fresh evocation.

verdict.trueWording: "almost a shorthand for description… instead of evoking it for us"
verdict.note: Page: "'Black as night' triggers vision only because it takes longer to read. It's almost a shorthand for description, Martin reminding us to picture the color black instead of evoking it for us. And that's simply because 'black as night' is familiar to us, and we are cognitively lazy with the familiar." Every element of the claim — shorthand, reliance on familiarity, absence of fresh evocation — is present. The embedded fragment "black as night" is verbatim; the surrounding sentence is a paraphrase. Four Martin instances are quoted as evidence.

claim: Dialogue is the part of Martin's prose that shines brightest, outclassing the narrative passages.

verdict.trueWording: "no surprise that dialogue would shine brightest"; other prose "forgettable"
verdict.note: Page: "all of the top answers referred to passages of dialogue… it's no surprise that dialogue would shine brightest. But the prose that constitutes the other 60% of the text is forgettable." "shine brightest" is verbatim; the claim's "outclassing the narrative passages" is the essay's "the other 60%… is forgettable". Note the essay grounds this in a Reddit thread of readers' favourite passages, not purely its own judgement.

claim: Martin (as quoted by the essay) prioritises getting the flow right in the draft over machining individual sentences.
source: At Sea Journal (anonymous, undated), quoting Martin

verdict.trueWording: "The flow is important, it's gotta come out right for him"
verdict.note: ATTRIBUTION IS OFF — substance holds, the sourcing does not. The flow-over-machining framing is the ESSAYIST's, not Martin's quoted words: "When he describes his writing process, he stresses rhythm"; "The flow is important, it's gotta come out right for him"; and of textualists, "These writers machine their sentences, plane and calibrate them… This is not Martin's way." The actual Martin block quote (January Magazine) says nothing about flow versus sentences — it is about good and bad writing days ("sometimes you eat the bear and sometimes the bear eats you"). So "as quoted by the essay" should be "as characterised by the essay". Counter-evidence worth knowing: the sibling page (imprecision.html) quotes Martin describing exactly the machining the claim denies — "trimming and tightening line by line and word by word… Finish the book, then go through it, cutting, cutting, cutting" — though he frames that as a final polish stage, not drafting.

claim: Some similes misdescribe the physical property they invoke, such as men vanishing like melting snow though snow melts slowly.

verdict.trueWording: "Snows melt slowly, over weeks and months. Mist evaporates quickly"
verdict.note: Exact match of substance. The page quotes the mountain clans "descending from the heights to rob and kill and melting away like snow whenever the knights rode out from the Vale", then comments: "Snows melt slowly, over weeks and months. Mist evaporates quickly, or smoke." The claim's "men vanishing like melting snow though snow melts slowly" is an accurate restatement.

claim: Near-synonymous modifiers are stacked without purpose ('low, quiet voice').

verdict.trueWording: "I extend this imprecision to his occasional redundancies" — "low, quiet voice"
verdict.note: Page: "I extend this imprecision to his occasional redundancies. These may happen because he's so focused on the target he's not sure which arrows he's pulling from the quiver", followed by the example "Jon told his uncle in a low, quiet voice." The parenthetical fragment "low, quiet voice" is verbatim. Four further examples of the same shape are listed ("a careful, measuring look"; "low, hushed voices"; "deep and sonorous"; "loved… all the things he loved"). The essay's term is "redundancies", not "doubled modifiers", and it says "occasional" — the claim's "without purpose" is the essayist's diagnosis of unintended repetition, which is fair.

claim: The prologue hammers one sensory note (cold) so often that the essayist wants half of it cut.

verdict.trueWording: "I need about 50% less about the cold here"
verdict.note: LOCATION IS WRONG — fix before use. The quoted line is exact: "I need about 50% less about the cold here." But the two passages it introduces are NOT the prologue: they are Jon at Castle Black ("Chunks of coal burned in iron braziers", "the roughspun blacks that were their everyday wear", "There was scant warmth to be found in Castle Black"), remembering Winterfell. The word "prologue" appears nowhere in the file, and AGOT's prologue is the Will/Waymar Royce ranging beyond the Wall. The cold-hammering observation is genuine; "the prologue" should read "a Jon chapter at Castle Black". Related but separate: the essay makes a second single-sense point immediately after, on anger being alternately cold and "flaring hot".

claim: Abstract emotion is figured with contradictory sensory vehicles (rage described as cold in one place and hot in another).

verdict.trueWording: Anger is sometimes cold too. Except when it is flaring hot.
verdict.note: Directly supported. The essay makes this exact point as an imprecision item, then quotes the Castle Black exchange containing 'Jon's anger flared', 'Jon said icily', and 'Jon was cold with rage' — hot and cold vehicles for the same emotion in one passage.

claim: 'Words are wind' is repeated through A Dance with Dragons to the point of excess.

verdict.trueWording: "Words are wind," is oft-repeated, probably a little bit too much.
verdict.note: Supported. Whitehead lists it under the book's deeds-not-words theme, and the closing paragraph calls out 'some over-used terms' among the book's dents.

claim: Martin holds a fairly strict one-character-per-chapter limited third person, rotating across chapters.

verdict.trueWording: Martin employs a fairly strict POV structure this time around.
verdict.note: Partial — read the caveat. The page supports chapters being allotted per POV character and rotating ('Dany, Jon and Tyrion … get a significant number of chapters each but everyone else only gets a few'; 'other POVs only show up when needed'; a 'busy, revolving-door feeling'). But 'fairly strict' on the page means strictness about WHICH characters get chapters, not strictness of narrative technique, and the review never mentions third person or limited narration. The claim borrows the page's exact adjective for a proposition the page does not state.

claim: Secondary-character chapters move fast with little or no filler.

verdict.trueWording: with these 'lesser' POVs, there's little to no time for filler
verdict.note: Supported, and reinforced by the adjacent 'gives some individual storylines and chapters a rather concise, focused feel'. The review adds the converse for the major POVs: Martin occasionally 'dwells on a story point a bit too long'.

claim: Martin visibly relishes certain long descriptive passages, such as the account of the Doom of Valyria.

verdict.trueWording: Martin seems to relish some descriptive passages.
verdict.note: Supported, with the Doom of Valyria named as the example: 'A detailed account of the Doom of Valyria – quite a few books overdue – is spine-crawling and disturbing.' The page says 'detailed', not 'long'; length is the claim's addition.

claim: The book breaks off on a series of stacked cliffhangers rather than closure.

verdict.trueWording: Martin breaks off the book on a series of titanic cliffhangers
verdict.note: Supported and near-verbatim; the page continues 'that dwarf anything seen previously, and only a few story threads find any sense of resolution.' One qualifier the claim drops: Whitehead says the final chapters still make the ending 'impressive, despite the cliffhangers'.

claim: The rotating-POV structure can frustrate because the reader is pulled away just as they settle into a viewpoint.

verdict.trueWording: The rotating-POV structure can lead to frustration
verdict.note: Supported almost exactly: '…as you are just settling into one character's storyline and are then wrenched halfway across the continent to another character and by the time you get back to the first one it's moved on by several weeks or months.' Listed under the book's flaws.

claim: Weeks pass between chapters and armies cover hundreds of miles offstage, giving the narrative rapid forward motion.

verdict.trueWording: sometimes weeks passing between chapters, armies covering hundreds of miles
verdict.note: The descriptive half is near-verbatim ('armies covering hundreds of miles in the blink of an eye'). The valence is flipped, though: the page files this under flaws — 'The book also feels like it moves a little too quickly at times' — rather than praising rapid forward motion. Whitehead does concede 'On one level this is a good thing', so the claim is not contradicted, only re-coloured.

claim: Individual locations such as the Red Keep, Winterfell and the Wall are made to come alive through description.

verdict.trueWording: individual locations like the Red Keep … come to life quite nicely
verdict.note: Supported with all three named locations (Red Keep, Winterfell, the Wall). Context worth keeping: this is a concession inside a criticism — the worldbuilding overall 'feels a little sketchy at this point', with the locations coming to life as the exception.

claim: Each point-of-view has its own distinct palette and purpose, and the interior life of characters is conveyed exceptionally well.

verdict.trueWording: each point-of-view having a distinct palette and purpose
verdict.note: Both halves supported in one sentence: 'His ability to convey the interior life of his characters is phenomenal, with each point-of-view having a distinct palette and purpose.' Byline and date on the page match: Matt Maenpaa, July 22, 2011.

claim: Martin does not rush; the prose favours response and interiority over action and is never concise.

verdict.trueWording: less about the actions … more about response, reaction and decision
verdict.note: All three parts supported: 'He does not rush'; 'no one has ever accused George R. R. Martin of being concise'; and the response-over-action sentence quoted here. Interiority is carried by 'His ability to convey the interior life of his characters is phenomenal.'

claim: Elaborately sensory feast descriptions serve to distract from and offset the wholesale slaughter.

verdict.trueWording: Martin distracts from the wholesale slaughter … with incredible sensory feasts
verdict.note: Near-verbatim: 'one of the ways Martin distracts from the wholesale slaughter is with incredible sensory feasts.' The page says 'distracts from'; 'offset' is the claim's addition but is a fair gloss. Byline and date match: Michael R. Underwood, July 27, 2013.

claim: Like Wagner, Martin gives each character recurring phrases that function as leitmotifs, kept close like dragons' eggs.

verdict.trueWording: Like Wagner, he gives each of his characters leitmotifs that recur
verdict.note: Supported, including the dragons'-eggs image: 'These phrases are like dragons' eggs: the characters keep them close, in the hopes that one day … the words will hatch forth the wisdom they desperately need.' Examples given are 'You know nothing, Jon Snow' and Daenerys' 'If I look back I am lost'. Sourcing caveat: time.com returns HTTP 406 to a direct fetch and the one Wayback capture of this URL is a 403, so text came via WebFetch; I ran a second adversarial pass with an explicit NOT-PRESENT option and both passes agreed on these fragments. Byline confirmed: Lev Grossman, Jul 7, 2011.

claim: Each storyline is written in its own voice, each playing off the others.

verdict.trueWording: each with its own rhythm, written in its own voice
verdict.note: Supported, from the count of storylines: '11 major story lines, as well as assorted minor ones, each with its own rhythm, written in its own voice, and each playing off all the others.' The claim drops 'its own rhythm'. Same fetch caveat as 118 — direct fetch 406, text via two agreeing WebFetch passes.

claim: Grossman rates the prose itself as deft and a pleasure in its own right, not merely a vehicle for plot.

verdict.trueWording: forgoing the great pleasure of Martin's deft prose
verdict.note: Grossman (byline Lev Grossman, Jul 7 2011) writes: "If you're watching A Game of Thrones on HBO, you're forgoing the great pleasure of Martin's deft prose." That treats the prose as a distinct pleasure the plot-bearing adaptation cannot supply, which is the claim's substance. Caveat on evidence quality: time.com refused direct fetch (HTTP 406) and the only Wayback capture of this URL is a 403, so the page was read through a summarizing fetch; the sentence was independently corroborated by a Slate review roundup quoting it. No word-for-word check of the whole article was possible.

claim: Martin's register is grounded and realist, men and women slugging it out in the muck, against Tolkien's elevated romance.

verdict.trueWording: men and women slugging it out in the muck
verdict.note: Full sentence: "It's men and women slugging it out in the muck, for money and power and lust and love," preceded by "A Feast for Crows isn't pretty elves against gnarly orcs." The muck phrase and the grounded/realist register are exact. The Tolkien contrast is real but framed as moral complexity, not register: "Tolkien's work has enormous imaginative force, but you have to go elsewhere for moral complexity." The words "elevated romance" are the claim's gloss, not Grossman's.

claim: The prose holds epic sweep and tiny touching human drama at the same time.

verdict.trueWording: epic sweep and tiny, touching human drama simultaneously
verdict.note: Source: "Martin has an astonishing ability to focus on epic sweep and tiny, touching human drama simultaneously." Attributed to Martin's ability generally rather than to "the prose" specifically, and the sentence sits beside praise of him as "a tense, surging, insomnia-inflicting plotter and a deft and inexhaustible sketcher of personalities." Substance holds; the word "prose" is the claim's.

claim: The supernatural appears only rarely, which keeps the texture close to historical fiction.

verdict.trueWording: The supernatural plays a role, but only rarely.
verdict.note: First half is essentially verbatim — the sentence appears exactly as "The supernatural plays a role, but only rarely." The second half is not in this source: Grossman never says the restraint keeps the texture close to historical fiction, and the words "historical fiction" do not appear in the article at all. If the historical-fiction link is needed, cite Fiction Advocate instead, which says Martin "uses fantastic elements sparingly... he initially conceived of the books as historical fiction."

claim: Bran I opens on a description of the season and weather, defying the usual advice against weather openings.

verdict.trueWording: advice trope of never opening with weather... applies here though
verdict.note: Both factual halves check out: the post quotes the opening line "The morning had dawned clear and cold, with a crispness that hinted at the end of summer" and calls it "A boring description of the weather?" But the polarity is the opposite of what "defying" implies. Auerbach writes that the advice "stands applies here though, so I've taken the liberty of excising it," then quotes the paragraph without the weather line and says "Much better." He treats it as a flaw Martin got away with, not a rule successfully broken. Do not cite this as endorsement of a weather opening.

claim: The first chapter is filtered through a seven-year-old attending his first beheading, so adult explanation arrives naturally.

verdict.trueWording: a seven-year old boy going to his first beheading
verdict.note: The core is directly supported: "We've got a seven-year old boy going to his first beheading," and the quoted passage gives "This was the first time he had been deemed old enough to go with his lord father..." The craft rationale is NOT in the source — Auerbach never discusses point of view, never says the child POV licenses adult explanation, and never connects the narrator's age to exposition. His nearest statement is only "this chapter actually accomplishes a lot. We learn a bit about the world and its history." The "so adult explanation arrives naturally" clause is the claim's own inference.

claim: Temporal facts (year of summer, Bran's age) are embedded in the opening paragraphs, and endgame hints are planted in a single paragraph.

verdict.trueWording: amazing how many hints G.R.R.M. dropped in one paragraph
verdict.note: Both halves supported. Time-stamps: the post quotes "It was the ninth year of summer, and the seventh of Bran's life" and comments "it's apparently the ninth year of summer." Endgame hints in a single paragraph: of the Old Nan paragraph he writes "it's amazing how many hints G.R.R.M. dropped in one paragraph" — Mance Rayder, the wildlings, and "the Others (the White Walkers) and the Long Night, which are incredibly important to the endgame of the entire series."

claim: Exposition is paired with a small dramatic tension so the reader is not lost during information delivery.

verdict.trueWording: pairing the exposition with the dramatic
verdict.note: Two supporting sentences: "the plot points allow for exposition to happen seamlessly, without losing the reader's interest" and "By pairing the exposition with the dramatic, you reduce the chances of losing the reader." Oliver's framing is "multiple small sources of tension" (Others, Bran's fall, Khal Drogo; and the Nabokov Pnin parallel), which matches the claim's "small dramatic tension."

claim: Names and a heavy (over)use of meaningful nicknames do exposition work across the large cast.

verdict.trueWording: his extreme (over)use of meaningful nicknames
verdict.note: Source: "Since Martin has a large cast, he has to use additional tools, such as his emphasis on the importance of names and his extreme (over)use of meaningful nicknames." The parenthetical "(over)use of meaningful nicknames" is verbatim, and the large-cast/exposition framing is explicit in the same sentence.

claim: Symbolic foreshadowing is planted openly early (a direwolf killed by a stag) and later events retroactively recontextualise tiny asides.

verdict.trueWording: obvious foreshadowing with a direwolf who's been killed by a stag
verdict.note: Both halves near-verbatim. Early and open: "then some obvious foreshadowing with a direwolf who's been killed by a stag" (repeated later as "the aforementioned obvious foreshadowing of the direwolf killed by a stag"). Retroactive recontextualising: "events retroactively reshape characters, they contextualize miniscule asides, and they illuminate the reader's understanding." Note the author's point is that the obviousness "doesn't matter" because the work does not rely on surprise.

claim: Martin says his aim was a book combining the best traits of contemporary fantasy with those of the historical novel.
source: George R.R. Martin, interviewed by Dylan Runco & Joanna Buffum, New Jersey Monthly, 2013-03-15

verdict.trueWording: combines some of the best traits of contemporary fantasy
verdict.note: Martin's own answer, near-verbatim: "One of the things I wanted to do was to write a book that combines some of the best traits of contemporary fantasy with some of the traits of the historical novel." He continues that historical fiction "had an excitement to it and a grittiness and a realness to it that the fantasy novels lacked" and that he wanted "to almost write a historical novel about history that never happened." Only softening: the source says "some of the traits of the historical novel," not "the best traits" of both.

claim: Martin says he loves describing food and values the small character-driven scenes over plot mechanics.
source: George R.R. Martin, New Jersey Monthly, 2013-03-15

verdict.trueWording: not the stuff that advances the plot, but... character parts
verdict.note: SPLIT — one half is misattributed. "Loves describing food" is the interviewer's premise ("NJM: ...we know from your writing that you love describing food"); Martin's reply is about missing Bayonne pizza and bar pies, and he never says he loves describing food. The second half IS Martin's own words: on cut scenes he says "it's a character scene, and mostly that's what has been cut, not the stuff that advances the plot, but the little character parts," and wishes for more episodes so "we could get in a lot more of these small character scenes." Cite only the character-scene half to Martin.

claim: In the cookbook foreword Martin says 'gratuitous' just means more than a given reader wanted, that fiction is emotion rather than intellect, and that he wants readers to taste the food.
source: George R.R. Martin, foreword to The Official Game of Thrones Cookbook, quoted by Nicole Drum, ComicBook.com, 2024-05-04
quote: I want them to taste the food.

verdict.trueWording: I want them to taste the food.
verdict.note: Supplied quote appears word for word, as the close of "When they sit down at my table, I want them to taste the food." All three sub-claims check out in the quoted foreword: "'gratuitous' usually translates to 'more than I wanted' or 'did not advance the plot'"; "Fiction is about emotion. The heart, not the head." Note the wording is "more than I wanted" (the critic's want), which the claim renders as "more than a given reader wanted" — a fair reading, but not the literal phrase. The article quotes the foreword via Polygon, so this is second-hand from the primary text.

claim: Martin frames dense description as the journey mattering more than the destination.
source: George R.R. Martin, cookbook foreword, via ComicBook.com, 2024-05-04

verdict.trueWording: It's not the destination that matters to me, it's the journey
verdict.note: Martin's foreword, quoted: "It's not the destination that matters to me, it's the journey," given directly as his answer to why the heraldry, the sex scenes and "the feasts, oh those feasts" are not cut — i.e. the dense description the claim names. One wrinkle: ComicBook's own paraphrase softens it to "the journey is as important as the destination," while Martin's quoted words say the journey matters and the destination does not. The claim tracks Martin, not the paraphrase.

claim: Martin defends blazon-level heraldic detail (his example: seven golden hedgehogs on dark green) as never gratuitous, wanting readers to live the story rather than read it.
source: George R.R. Martin, cookbook foreword, via Dan Selcke, Winter Is Coming

verdict.trueWording: I want them to live my story, not just read it
verdict.note: Both halves land. Martin's foreword asks whether it was necessary to mention the knight who 'bore seven golden hedgehogs on a field of dark green' — the claim's 'on dark green' drops 'on a field of', so not verbatim. 'Nothing is gratuitous, as I see it' appears exactly.

claim: Meals carry narrative purpose (Walder Frey's deliberately dull dinner as an insult) and are coloured by the POV character's emotion.

verdict.trueWording: more often than not, they serve a narrative purpose
verdict.note: First half exact: Walder Frey 'is purposefully serving the King in the North a ho-hum dinner ... as a small act of discourtesy'. The POV-emotion half is the weaker leg: supported by instances ('flavored with fear'; 'the calves' brains turned Catelyn's stomach') but the page never states it as a general principle.

claim: Food passages use unfamiliar culinary terms that stretch the reader's vocabulary, and certain food phrasings recur verbatim (warm bread from the kitchens).

verdict.trueWording: warm bread, fresh from the kitchens
verdict.note: Vocabulary half exact: 'I routinely come across food terms I've never seen before. Capon. Trencher. Lamprey pie' plus 'expanding my vocabulary'. Recurrence half: 'One of Martin's most repeated phrases is...' — the claim's 'warm bread from the kitchens' omits 'fresh', so not verbatim.

claim: Martin credits his Hollywood years with teaching him structure and dialogue, and says he builds the world alongside the prose rather than first.
source: George R.R. Martin (Rolling Stone 2014, Mikal Gilmore) as digested by Karen Woodward, 2014-04-25

verdict.trueWording: Being there improved my sense of structure and dialogue
verdict.note: Both halves are direct Martin quotes on the page. Worldbuilding: 'I don't build the world first, then write in it. I just write the story, and then put it together.' Correctly sourced to the Rolling Stone / Mikal Gilmore interview as digested by Woodward.

claim: Martin uses real names still in use (Robert) rather than invented fantasy names, and cannot write a character until the right name is found.
source: George R.R. Martin, reported by Dan Dalton, BuzzFeed, 2014-08-20

verdict.trueWording: I took actual names we still use today, like 'Robert'
verdict.note: Both halves present. Martin also disparages invented names ('A lot of fantasy names are too much'), and on the second half: 'If I can't find the right name I don't know who the character is and I can't proceed.'

claim: When one POV stalls, Martin switches to another character's chapter to keep drafting.
source: George R.R. Martin, reported by Dan Dalton, BuzzFeed, 2014-08-20

verdict.trueWording: run into a Tyrion problem, I can write with Arya
verdict.note: Appears under the heading 'On overcoming blocks': 'Thankfully, I have a lot of characters. So if I run into a Tyrion problem, I can write with Arya for a while.'

claim: Martin holds that the best fantasy is written in the language of dreams, prizing sensory and emotional vividness.
source: George R.R. Martin, The Faces of Fantasy (1996), via Wikiquote

verdict.trueWording: The best fantasy is written in the language of dreams
verdict.note: Exact word-for-word match on Wikiquote, and the attribution line beneath the passage reads 'The Faces of Fantasy (1996)' as claimed. The 'sensory and emotional vividness' clause is a fair paraphrase of the following catalogue (silver and scarlet; tastes of habaneros and honey).

claim: Each chapter is seen through one character's knowledge and prejudices; schemers like Varys and Littlefinger are denied POV to preserve mystery, and the prologue uses a disposable viewpoint.

verdict.trueWording: perspectives of mysterious people (like Varys or Petyr Baelish)
verdict.note: All three parts hold: 'we kind of see it through that character's biases'; POV withheld from schemers 'because that would ruin the mystery'; and the prologue's Will 'never shows up again'. The page names Petyr Baelish rather than 'Littlefinger'.

claim: Chapters are headed by the viewpoint character's name and the POV is never broken within a chapter.

verdict.trueWording: Each chapter is named after its POV character
verdict.note: Both halves explicit; 'while never breaking the rule within a chapter' appears word for word, though the claim's surrounding phrasing is a paraphrase. Byline and date confirmed: Faye Lennox, Mar 14, 2026.

claim: Simile is the predominant figure of speech, with personification of natural forces and frequent tonal shifts.

verdict.trueWording: simile was the most predominant figurative language used
verdict.note: All three parts hold. Personification section: 'the winter is a living beast that devours anyone not ready for it'; tonal shifts traced across fear, looming danger, agitation, fright. Byline 'written by Joshua Ehiosun' confirmed.

claim: In the prologue the sudden onset of cold and the scream-like sound of clashing swords serve as sensory signals of the supernatural.

verdict.trueWording: Suddenly, it becomes cold; swords clash, a sound like a scream
verdict.note: Both sensory details are on the page essentially verbatim and both sit against the Others' appearance. Caveat: this is LitCharts' summary column; the visible analysis reads the prologue for leadership and climate change, not as 'sensory signals of the supernatural' — that gloss is the claimant's inference, and the adjacent analysis panes are paywalled placeholder text.

claim: Bran I's first line sets the bleak execution scene and hints at summer's end, and the child POV licenses adult explanation.
source: Tommy E. Turner, The Fantasy Reviews, 2023-10-19

verdict.trueWording: sets the stage for the immediate bleak scene of execution
verdict.note: Content verified both halves: first line quoted with 'a crispness that hinted at the end of summer', and the child POV 'allows George R.R. Martin the space to explain a few things'. Attribution is off: page metadata gives the author as 'fantasyreviews' (not Tommy E. Turner) and the site as 'The Fantasy Review'; datePublished 2023-10-19 matches.

claim: The five published books run to more than 1.7 million words in 344 chapters (73/70/82/46/73), roughly 5,000 words per chapter (my arithmetic from the page's figures).

verdict.trueWording: 1,736,054 words, 344 chapters; 5,047 words per chapter
verdict.note: Verified via Wayback (2026-02-10) — the live host returned HTTP 454 browser challenge. Table matches exactly: 73/70/82/46/73, summing to 344, and 'more than 1.7 million words' is verbatim. Arithmetic checks: 1,736,054/344 = 5,046.7, so 'roughly 5,000' is sound and is correctly flagged as the claimant's own derivation. Byline Danny McLoughlin and original date Oct 19, 2021 confirmed; the snapshot shows an update of July 8, 2025, so the claimed 2026-03-27 update postdates my capture and is unconfirmed.

claim: Martin combines archaic expressions with modern language and seeds specific coined terms (warg, pyromancer).

verdict.trueWording: combines archaic expressions with modern language
verdict.note: Exact match: 'Martin skillfully combines archaic expressions with modern language.' The coinages clause paraphrases 'Martin introduces specific terms like "warg" and "pyromancer"'. Byline Jack Zhang and date 2025-01-15 both confirmed.

Author and date (Cinthia Koeksal, February 22, 2013) confirmed.

claim: Martin systematically excludes Latin-, Greek-, and French-derived and neoclassical vocabulary in favour of short Anglo-Saxon-origin words.

Conclusion repeats it: "Latinate words or affixes... are mostly excluded or only deployed for effect".

claim: His prefixes are native English (un-, be-, and the archaic positional a-) and his suffixes overwhelmingly Old English (-craft, -dom, -hood, -less, -ling, -ship, -ward), while Latinate -able/-ate/-ion/-ous are rare.

One qualifier: "-able, -ate, -ion, -ous, -ure" appear on the page as the general inventory of Latin suffixes in English, not in a sentence calling those four rare in Martin; rarity is asserted for Latinate affixes as a class.

claim: Martin builds well over a hundred two-root compounds from short native words and coins his world-vocabulary by the same compounding.

verdict.trueWording: (ironborn, sellsword, ravencraft), to the... inspired (weirwood, greensight, skinchanger)
verdict.note: The five words all appear but NOT as the contiguous string quoted — they sit in two separate parenthetical groups, in a different order, split by "ravencraft". So not verbatim. The "well over a hundred" figure is also not stated on the page: it is supported by counting the article's own Feast For Crows list, which runs ~152 compounds (aftertaste... woodharp). claim: The medieval-fantasy feel comes from the frequency of compounds rather than from any single coinage.

Anglo-Saxon vocabulary.' Two calibrations: the post's stated contrast is systematic Anglo-Saxon vocabulary versus stock phrases, not compounds versus 'any single coinage'; and compounds are explicitly 'just one of the verbal techniques.' The word 'cumulative' does not appear on this page (it appears in the 2014 post's conclusion).

claim: The style veers between functional modern thriller prose and prose padded with fake medievalisms, sometimes on the same page.

verdict.trueWording: veers from purely functional modern thriller prose

claim: Martin's baseline register is plain and functional, with periodic flashes of limpid beauty, notably in Arya's chapters.

verdict.trueWording: The default setting of Martin's style is lucid and functional

I particularly associate this with the character of Arya Stark once she's set sail from Westeros.'
