claim: He repeats a small set of words within a passage (cool, still) to build stillness and mood.
quote: repetitions in this passage – of 'cool' and 'still'

verdict.trueWording: repetitions in this passage – of 'cool' and 'still'
verdict.note: Quotation is exact (en dash and curly quotes as printed). CAVEAT ON THE CLAIM, not the quote: the source explicitly refuses to settle the purpose the claim asserts — 'I can't decide whether the repetitions in this passage... are signs of haste, or careful repetitions designed to evoke the lazy, torpid atmosphere of Lord Martell's sea retreat.' The claim's 'to build stillness and mood' states as fact one of two alternatives the author leaves open, and the source's word is 'lazy, torpid atmosphere,' not stillness. Treat the purposive reading as the citing author's inference.

claim: Confrontations are carried by short, charged exchanges that deliver the revelations rather than by narration.
quote: terse, charged dialogue

verdict.trueWording: Confrontations between opposing characters are done though terse, charged dialogue
verdict.note: Exact match under heading '4 Dramatic dialogue' (the source's 'though' for 'through' is its own typo, outside the quoted span). 'Deliver the revelations' is supported: 'you experience a real dramatic shock when you realise, along with one character, the implications of another one's words.' The contrastive 'rather than by narration' is the citing author's framing; the page does not state that contrast.

claim: He makes familiar words strange by slight deformation and adds wholly coined medieval-sounding words (sellsword, smallfolk).
quote: slight deformation of existing standard words or phrases

verdict.trueWording: the slight deformation of existing standard words or phrases
verdict.note: Exact match under '5 Distorting English': 'Martin employs the slight deformation of existing standard words or phrases into something rich and strange.' The coinage half holds but the exemplars are mis-filed: sellsword and smallfolk appear under section 7, 'New word combinations' ('Martin uses this facility to coin scores of neologisms'), whereas section 6's 'completely new, medieval-sounding words' are sept/septon/septa, maester, wildlings, pyromancer, holdfast, warg, damphair. Both sections are coinage, so substance survives.

claim: The would-be medievalisms harden into mannerisms that annoy on repetition.
quote: would-be medievalisms which become annoying mannerisms

verdict.trueWording: would-be medievalisms which become annoying mannerisms
verdict.note: Exact match under '9. Cod medievalism': 'there is a number of would-be medievalisms which become annoying mannerisms.' The claim's 'on repetition' is a gloss; the page's own frequency language is 'all-too-frequently' and 'The most persistent one,' listing dropped -ly adverbs, 'oft', 'elsewise', 'amongst/whilst', 'much and more'.

claim: Martin reuses fixed descriptors like a Homeric epithet system, with 'black as night' appearing four times nearly unchanged.
source: At Sea Journal (Erik Germani), 'The American Homer'
quote: Stock phrases are thermals

verdict.trueWording: stock phrases are thermals
verdict.note: Exact match, mid-sentence and lowercase: 'Style doesn't matter so much as lift, and stock phrases are thermals.' The rest of the claim is confirmed independently: the essay opens with Homeric epithets ('Dawn is always rosy-fingered; Athena is grey-eyed'), and quotes 'black as night' from four separate passages — Ice's blade in 'waters black as night', dragon 'scales were black as night', bastards' 'hair as black as night', Mirri Maz Duur's 'eyes as black as night'. Four instances, near-identical, as claimed.

claim: No single sentence is especially strong; the prose works by volley, which the author calls shotgun writing.
source: At Sea Journal (Erik Germani), 'The American Homer'
quote: No single sentence is that effective

verdict.trueWording: no single sentence is that effective
verdict.note: Exact match: 'It's shotgun writing: like buckshot, no single sentence is that effective, but a full cartridge of it gets the point across.' 'Shotgun writing' is the author's own term, as the claim states, and 'low-density sentences' is likewise his phrase ('a steady flow of low-density sentences'). 'Works by volley' is a fair paraphrase of the buckshot/full-cartridge image.

claim: Stock phrases work by triggering recognition rather than fresh visualisation, which keeps the reading fast.
source: At Sea Journal (Erik Germani), 'The American Homer'
quote: We are cognitively lazy with the familiar.

verdict.trueWording: we are cognitively lazy with the familiar
verdict.note: Exact match, mid-sentence and lowercase: 'And that's simply because "black as night" is familiar to us, and we are cognitively lazy with the familiar.' Recognition-over-visualisation is supported by the preceding lines: '"Black as night" triggers vision only because it takes longer to read... Martin reminding us to picture the color black instead of evoking it for us.' The speed point rests on 'an almost hypnotic readability' and 'you never have to read an AGOT sentence twice.'

claim: Character speech is consistently more memorable than the surrounding narrative description.
source: At Sea Journal (Erik Germani), 'The American Homer'
quote: Dialogue would shine brightest

verdict.trueWording: it's no surprise that dialogue would shine brightest
verdict.note: Exact match: 'In a series so focused on character and written by an author with an ear for it, it's no surprise that dialogue would shine brightest. But the prose that constitutes the other 60% of the text is forgettable.' The page grounds it in a Reddit thread on favourite passages where 'all of the top answers referred to passages of dialogue.'

claim: Bodies and moods are rendered through a recurring kit of phrases (faces still as masks, men corded with muscle).
source: At Sea Journal (Erik Germani), 'The American Homer'
quote: Faces still as masks, faces dark with anger

verdict.trueWording: those faces still as masks, and the faces dark with anger
verdict.note: NOT verbatim as given. The page reads 'the real Martinian stock phrases are those faces still as masks, and the faces dark with anger' — the supplied quote deletes 'and the' and capitalises 'Faces'. The second exemplar is also loose: the page has 'all those men corded or thick with muscle,' not 'men corded with muscle'. The recurring-kit substance is fully supported (the same sentence continues with 'chins dripping with hot juices', 'muscled like a bovid', 'hair shines like spun gold').

claim: Martin hovers close at the character's shoulder but steps back to narratorial distance at odd moments, mixing the character's word for a person with the narrator's full name in one paragraph.
source: At Sea Journal (Erik Germani), 'The Unseen Plane Crash: Psychic Distance'
quote: take[s] a big step backwards at odd times

verdict.trueWording: only to take a big step backwards at odd times
verdict.note: The page reads 'He's generally hovering right over his POV's shoulders... only to take a big step backwards at odd times.' The quote's '[s]' correctly marks the inflection change, and the underlying words match exactly. The second half is supported by the worked example: in the Tyrion breakfast passage, 'Pups' is Tyrion's word while 'Jaime Lannister' is not — '"Pups" sounds like a term Tyrion would use, but Tyrion wouldn't call his brother Jaime Lannister... that's Martin talking.'

claim: An evaluative adverb in narration ('Stupidly, Jon argued') fuses narrator judgment with the character's own.
quote: Stupidly, Jon argued

verdict.trueWording: Stupidly, Jon argued.
verdict.note: Exact match, quoted from AGOT: 'Stupidly, Jon argued. "I'll be fifteen on my name day," he said.' CAVEAT ON THE CLAIM: the essay poses this as an open question rather than asserting fusion — its lead-in is 'In this next quote, who thinks Jon is being stupid? Jon, or the narrator?' — and files it under 'Martin does not always control psychic distance.' 'Fuses narrator judgment with the character's own' is the citing author's resolution of an ambiguity the source deliberately leaves standing.

claim: Italicised thought grew by roughly six percent across the series and is weakest when it states the obvious or jogs memory.

verdict.trueWording: Is a 6 percent increase that big a deal?
verdict.note: No quote supplied. The figure is on the page: 'You might shrug at those proportions. Is a 6 percent increase that big a deal? Absolutely.' Growth across the series is supported by 'there's more of it with every book' and an embedded chart (img alt='italics over time'). The weakness half is near-exact: 'those italicized bits are Martin at his kludgiest. He uses them to jog the reader's memory, wedge in a pile of backstory, or point out the obvious.' One caveat: the 6 percent refers to proportions displayed in the chart image, which the page's text never itself tabulates, and the author flags a measurement disclaimer (he assumes italics are a consistent proxy for interior monologue).

claim: Calling one person 'her father', 'Ned Stark', 'Father', and 'Eddard Stark' within a scene signals unsteady narrative distance.

verdict.trueWording: Martin cycles through every possible nomination for Ned
verdict.note: No quotation was supplied, so verbatim status cannot be granted. The psychic_distance essay introduces the excerpt as 'For another good example of shifting psychic distance, here's a scene in which Martin cycles through every possible nomination for Ned,' and the quoted passage contains all four namings the claim lists: 'Her father had been fighting with the council again', 'when Ned Stark strode into the Small Hall', 'said when Father entered', and 'Be seated, Eddard Stark said.' The essay's gloss is 'in Sansa/Arya chapters Ned goes by "her father" or "Father". It's distracting to see it every other way.' Elsewhere it also states that 'Eddard Stark' is 'a marker of narrative distance.' Minor internal wrinkle in the source, not in the claim: the essay calls it 'a Sansa chapter' though the excerpt narrates from Arya.

claim: A word like 'Even' in narration marks the POV character's perspective without an explicit thought tag.

verdict.trueWording: Even is being used as an intensifier
verdict.note: No quotation was supplied. The essay's numbered point 3 is exactly this: 'Even. If you take that from the third sentence, we're not sure if Sansa notices the noticing. But even assures us she does... Even is being used as an intensifier, like very and really, and objective narrators rarely use those... one more way for writers to mark psychic distance and create subjective voice.' The 'without an explicit thought tag' half is directly supported: the essay praises Martin for inflecting 'the narrative with Sansa's perspective without ever lapsing into those annoying italic monologues.' The example sentence is narration ('Even Septa Mordane noted her composure and nodded in approval'). One hedge the claim drops: the essay denies intensifiers are a hard rule, calling it 'just a useful convention.'

claim: A handful of relics (must needs, soon or late, near as) supply historical flavour in place of consistent period language.
quote: a few linguistic relics to give a historical veneer

verdict.trueWording: a few linguistic relics to give a historical veneer
verdict.note: Quotation appears word for word: 'Most fantasists settle for a few linguistic relics to give a historical veneer.' All three named relics are confirmed in the next sentence: 'Martin has a few of these, like the much-teased "must needs". There's also "soon or late", "pretend to surprise", and "near as" for "nearly as".' Note the quoted sentence is a generalization about fantasists, with Martin then given as an instance; the essay also allows a second option (period-unspecific formal diction) that the claim omits.

claim: Words such as pug-nosed, longshoreman (1811), condone (1857), yen, burp, and snark leak modern English into Westeros.
quote: shows you the seams of his work

verdict.trueWording: Martin shows you the seams of his work
verdict.note: Quotation appears word for word, in the snark passage: 'by using it in the exact same context, Martin shows you the seams of his work.' All six items check out: pug ('are there pugs in Westeros?', 'She was pug-nosed and bouncy'); 'Longshoreman came into English in 1811, according to Etymonline.com' (1811 exact); condone tied to 'the Matrimonial Causes Act, an 1857 piece of legislation' (1857 exact); yen 'is in fact about a hundred years old'; burp 'Only a few decades older than Martin' (charted 1932). Two precision notes: 1857 is the Act's date, the essay's explanation for the word taking hold in English, not an etymological first-use date; and snark is presented as a Lewis Carroll coinage rather than as modern English generally.

claim: Many sentences are modular and deletable: a 1,897-word passage compresses to 427 words using only topic sentences.
quote: modular sentences that can snap together like LEGO

verdict.trueWording: modular sentences that can snap together like LEGO
verdict.note: Quotation appears word for word. The figures are exact: 'Those seven paragraphs, totalling 427 words, are actually built from the first sentences of 26 different paragraphs, totalling 1,897 words.' Deletability is the essay's opening thesis: 'you can pull out quite a few sentences before they start getting wobbly.' Two directional notes: the essay assembled 427 words out of 1,897 rather than compressing a continuous passage, and the LEGO line is one of several speculative explanations ('Maybe... Or this is an epiphenomenon... Maybe it's...'), not an asserted finding.

claim: Frequent single-sentence paragraphs sustain narrative momentum.
quote: Martin has a fair number of one-lines

verdict.trueWording: (Martin has a fair number of one-lines.)
verdict.note: Quotation appears word for word, parenthetically. The momentum link is present but weaker than the claim states: the essay is hunting 'something beyond the plot that's contributing to the series' propulsiveness,' then offers 'Or this is an epiphenomenon, and the real driver is a short average paragraph. (Martin has a fair number of one-lines.)' So one-line paragraphs are floated as a possible driver among alternatives, and 'a fair number' is a softer quantity than the claim's 'Frequent'.

claim: Some similes misfire on tempo (brigands melting like snow) or on verb-modifier logic (glowering through a beard), and redundant paired adjectives recur.
quote: low, quiet voice

verdict.trueWording: Jon told his uncle in a low, quiet voice.
verdict.note: Quotation appears word for word in the redundancy list. All three components confirmed. Tempo: 'melting away like snow whenever the knights rode out,' glossed 'Snows melt slowly, over weeks and months. Mist evaporates quickly, or smoke.' Verb-modifier logic: 'He glowered at Arya through his thick beard,' glossed 'Glowering is a verb for watching, suggesting that his beard is covering his face.' Redundant pairs: 'I extend this imprecision to his occasional redundancies,' followed by 'low, quiet voice', 'careful, measuring look', 'low, hushed voices', 'slow, endless clanging'.

claim: Sentences devoted to coldness pile up and could be cut by about half.

verdict.trueWording: I need about 50% less about the cold here
verdict.note: No quotation was supplied, so verbatim status cannot be granted, but the page states the claim almost exactly. The imprecision essay interposes the line 'I need about 50% less about the cold here.' immediately before two Castle Black paragraphs stacked with cold sentences ('Jon found himself shivering. The chill was always with him here... So cold, he thought... the walls were cold here, and the people colder'), and continues the run with 'Anger is sometimes cold too. Except when it is flaring hot.' 'About half' matches 'about 50%' precisely.

claim: Around 250 zeugmatic sentences occur in roughly 148,130 sentences, most often about the body and about sky or weather.
source: At Sea Journal (Erik Germani), 'Zeugma and Literary DNA'
quote: The day was warm and cloudless, the sky a deep blue.

verdict.trueWording: The day was warm and cloudless, the sky a deep blue.
verdict.note: Quotation appears word for word. Both figures are exact and in one sentence: 'But Martin's written a lot of sentences for ASOIAF - 148,130 by my count - and when I checked for this structure I found ~250 examples of it.' The subject ranking is explicit: 'Those sky sentences represent a good portion of the total, but the most common subject is the human body.' The claim's 'roughly' and 'around' correctly mirror the essay's own '~250' and 'by my count', and the essay discloses its method ('My net caught any sentences with commas whose first word was repeated after the first comma').

claim: Mid-speech attribution and action beats are placed to work as extra punctuation and control the reader's ear; the ideal exchange is untagged.
quote: tags, when strategically placed, can serve as extra punctuation

verdict.trueWording: These tags, when strategically placed, can serve as extra punctuation
verdict.note: Quotation appears word for word as a substring of 'These tags, when strategically placed, can serve as extra punctuation.' Timing control follows immediately: 'It lets you play with the timing of a line,' illustrated by three mid-speech interruptions ('These dead were all strong men,' said Roger Ryswell, 'and none of them were stabbed.'). Action beats are covered by 'the speaker can make a quick gesture beforehand' and 'Or just after'. The untagged ideal is present but framed as opinion: 'I have the feeling, and I don't know if you agree, that the ideal dialogue exchange is untagged, back and forth.'

claim: In A Game of Thrones semicolons and colons are used interchangeably (three on one page), a habit corrected by A Dance with Dragons.
quote: he's gotten the semicolon figured out by now

verdict.trueWording: Seems like he's gotten the semicolon figured out by now
verdict.note: Quotation appears word for word. Opening sentence: 'In AGOT, Martin uses semicolons and colons interchangeably.' The page count is exact: 'Incredibly, there are three examples of this on one page, 239 in my edition of AGOT.' One softening the claim drops: the ADWD verdict is hedged and evidentially weak in the source, 'Seems like he's gotten the semicolon figured out by now, though, ADWD didn't pop any for me' - an absence of noticed instances by one reader, not a demonstrated correction.

feature: purple register for nature and violence
claim: The tone swings from casual to purple, with ornate diction reserved for wilderness (green) and bloodshed (red).
source: At Sea Journal (Erik Germani), 'Purple Prose in Green and Red'
quote: the tone can be very casual and very purple

verdict.trueWording: In ASOIAF, the tone can be very casual and very purple
verdict.note: Quotation appears word for word. The green/red framing is explicit: 'Here I'd like to point out Martin's reasons for using it: as an ecstatic response to nature and violence' and 'It's about the green and the red, for Martin.' Ornate diction is identified in the wilderness passage: 'Martin shifts into antiquated diction: "tangle of root and thorn and grasping limb"; "Knew not"; "small wonder".' Minor overstatement in the claim: the essay gives nature and violence as Martin's reasons for the high register, not as an exclusive reservation, and adds a second function - the register can 'capture the experience or distance the reader from it.'

claim: Combat passages personify the sword and stretch or stop time.
source: At Sea Journal (Erik Germani), 'Purple Prose in Green and Red'
quote: time slept when swords woke

verdict.trueWording: It might have been minutes or it might have been hours; time slept when swords woke
verdict.note: Quotation appears word for word. Time distortion is directly supported by that sentence and its lead-in, 'Jaime could not have said how long he pressed the attack.' Weapon animation is present in the combat material the essay quotes: 'the longsword alive in his hands', 'The swords kissed and sprang apart and kissed again', and 'the gilded sword that had sipped the blood of the last of the Dragonkings'. One attribution note: 'personify' is the claimant's analytic label, not the essayist's word; the essay makes its explicit self-animation point about axes in the wilderness passage ('He doesn't tell us who is swinging these few axes, they seem to swing themselves, as though enchanted').

claim: Backstory is delivered as monologue dressed as dialogue, assigned to talkative characters as a trait, lampshaded, or reported in summary rather than quoted.
source: At Sea Journal (Erik Germani), 'Now, As We All Know'
quote: It is a flashback dressed up as a monologue

verdict.trueWording: It is a flashback dressed up as a monologue
verdict.note: Quotation appears word for word, following Ned's roughly 650-word remembrance to Robert. All four mechanisms are confirmed. Trait assignment: 'Telling Catelyn stuff she already knows is Rodrik's thing... It's just a character trait!' and Hal Mollen, 'He had a penchant for loudly announcing the obvious.' Lampshading: 'Winking at the audience while doing something gauche (hanging a lampshade, as TvTropes would have it).' Summary over quotation: 'Sam Tarly's backstory feels better in comparison to the above, because Martin reports it instead of quoting directly.' One wording note: the claim inverts the essay's phrase - the source says flashback dressed up as a monologue, not monologue dressed as dialogue.

claim: Chapters cycle among coercion, negotiation, action, travel, revelation, predicament, and disclosure scenes, each shoehorning in secondary information.
quote: The narrative cycles between these types of scene.

verdict.trueWording: The narrative cycles between these types of scene.
verdict.note: Quotation appears word for word. Six of the seven types map directly to the essay's numbered list: coercion (1), 'Discussions/arguments about what to do/bargaining' (2), 'Action sequence' (3), 'Travelling sequence' (4), 'A predicament is sketched out' (6), 'Present information is disclosed' (7). The shoehorning half is explicit: 'Every chapter is like this. There is some central action to the scene, but Martin takes the opportunity to shoehorn in some other information.' One relabel to flag: the claim's 'revelation' stands for type 5, which the essay words as 'An enigma is laid out or an action is promised' - closer to a mystery posed or a promise made than to a revelation delivered.

claim: A chapter opens in medias res on a small crisis, slides from past perfect into simple past for a compressed memory, then returns to the present.
source: At Sea Journal (Erik Germani), 'The Short-Hop Flashback'
quote: past perfect melds into the simple past tense

verdict.trueWording: past perfect melds into the simple past tense
verdict.note: Exact string match. Essay quotes Reddit user Bookshelfstud describing the pattern (chapter opens 'in media res' on 'usually a small crisis', drops back for background, then 'the scene picks up again and resolves'), then illustrates with Tyrion's fifth chapter in the sky cell: 'Notice how the past perfect melds into the simple past tense.' Claim's full three-part structure is supported.

claim: Martin permits himself narratorial distance only when temporal distance justifies it.
source: At Sea Journal (Erik Germani), 'The Short-Hop Flashback'
quote: only with temporal distance will he permit himself some narrative distance

verdict.trueWording: Only with temporal distance will he permit himself some narrative distance
verdict.note: Word-for-word match; the page capitalizes 'Only' because it begins a sentence, the only difference from the submitted fragment. Context supports the claim exactly: 'His storytelling moment-to-moment is exactly that. Only with temporal distance will he permit himself some narrative distance.'

claim: Catchphrases and nicknames make thin characters stick (Walder Frey's heh, Hodor, Gregor's seventeen lines).
source: At Sea Journal (Erik Germani), 'Making a Memorable Character'
quote: Gregor Clegane: 17 lines

verdict.trueWording: Gregor Clegane: 17 lines
verdict.note: Exact string match, as a section heading in 'Making a Memorable Character'. Supporting elements all present: Walder Frey 'has a nickname (the Late Lord Frey), a catchphrase (heh)'; 'Hodor is memorable through repetition'; the essay's list of devices includes 'nicknames, monikers, AKAs' and 'catchphrases and speech patterns'. claim: Movement sentences chain prepositional phrases to carry the reader through space.

I even have a name for it: the moving sentence,' and pairs the Martin line with Katherine Mansfield's 'Away she skimmed, over the lawn, up the path...'. Claim's characterization as chained prepositional phrases carrying the reader through space is supported.

claim: Narration slips into the character's own idiom for a phrase, a move the essay flags as free indirect.

verdict.trueWording: A little free indirect!
verdict.note: Exact string match. It is the essay's one-line gloss immediately following the Catelyn passage 'She had begged Ned not to go, not now, not after what had happened; everything had changed now, couldn't he see that?' — narration in the character's own idiom, as the claim states.

claim: Double meanings are exploited in a single word (rams that lap at water).

verdict.trueWording: cruel iron rams lapping at the water
verdict.note: Exact string match. The essay's gloss confirms the claim's substance: 'that's an arresting conflation of the meaning of the siege implement and the bovid. What a neat way to exploit a homonym.' The double meaning sits on 'rams', triggered by 'lapping', exactly as the claim describes.

claim: Characters are built by others' talk long before they speak; Stannis is named 98 times before appearing.
source: At Sea Journal (Erik Germani), 'Your Reputation Precedes You'
quote: Stannis is mentioned 98 times before he appears

verdict.trueWording: Stannis is mentioned 98 times before he appears… in the second book!
verdict.note: Exact string match for the quoted fragment; the page continues '… in the second book!'. Minor nuance: the comparative's referent ('than epic fantasy') is implied by the surrounding Tolkien discussion rather than stated.

claim: Because history locks a writer in, Martin mixes sources and amplifies them, holding that fantasy must be bigger and brighter than life (Hadrian's Wall becomes seven hundred feet of ice).
source: SLF Portolan Project transcript, Mary Anne Mohanraj, Dublin (Aug 2019)
quote: fantasy always has to be a little bigger and brighter

verdict.trueWording: fantasy always has to be a little bigger and brighter
verdict.note: Same PDF. Verbatim: "the thing about historical fiction, why I don't write it, is because you're locked in by the history... So by using this as inspiration, but mixing and matching, taking a bit of this, a bit of that, and turning it up to eleven. I mean, fantasy always has to be a little bigger and brighter and more colorful than real life. So I can be inspired by Hadrian's Wall but Hadrian's Wall was like ten feet tall and my wall was like seven hundred feet tall, and made of ice." The 'turn it up to eleven' feature label and the Hadrian's Wall detail are both verbatim.

claim: Martin tells writers to think through every departure from real life (flying pigs change the pork industry) and to get armor, armies and horses right or readers will write.
source: SLF Portolan Project transcript, Mary Anne Mohanraj, Dublin (Aug 2019)
quote: it's gonna change the pork industry

verdict.trueWording: it's gonna change the pork industry
verdict.note: Same PDF. Verbatim: "if you're gonna make pigs fly, you know, it's gonna change the pork industry... So think through everything where you depart from real life... whether it's, you know, medieval armies, or armor and weaponry, or care and feeding of horses, or whatever it is, try to get it right. Because if you get it wrong, somebody will notice and write you letters about it." Armor, armies, horses and the reader letters are all present as claimed.

claim: Martin contrasts Dunsany's once-upon-a-time mode with Tolkien's dynastic history and places his own work with Tolkien, closer to historical fiction.
source: SLF Portolan Project transcript, Mary Anne Mohanraj, Dublin (Aug 2019)
quote: who was the king before him?

verdict.trueWording: who was the king before him?
verdict.note: Same PDF; the quoted string is Martin's, verbatim: of Dunsany, "And once upon a time there was a king and you know, he had a beautiful daughter and then an elf came in, but you don't get the sense of, 'Okay, what was the name of the dynasty this king was, who was the king before him? How did this dynasty come to power?'" ATTRIBUTION CAVEAT: the claim's second half — placing Martin's own work with Tolkien, closer to historical fiction — is spoken in the transcript by the interviewer Mary Anne Mohanraj ("Whereas what you're doing is closer, and Tolkien is closer, to historical fiction"), not by Martin, and no assent from Martin is recorded before the session wraps. Martin does independently support the substance elsewhere in the same transcript (Tolkien's 'immense construct underneath', "now I have a fair amount of ice under the surface", and wanting to meld epic fantasy with historical fiction), so the claim is defensible — but as worded it credits Martin with the interviewer's formulation.

claim: Martin says fantasy must be rooted in reality first, then played with and given its imaginative element.
source: Bullseye / Sound of Young America, John Hodgman (2011-09-19)
quote: In fantasy, you have to root it in reality.

verdict.trueWording: for doing fantasy, is you have to root it in reality
verdict.note: Transcript at maximumfun.org: "That's the general process for doing fantasy, is you have to root it in reality. Then you play with it a little; then you add the imaginative element, then you make it largely bigger." The claim's substance — root in reality, then play, then add the imaginative element — is supported in exact order, but the quoted sentence "In fantasy, you have to root it in reality." is a paraphrase and does not appear on the page. Fix the quote wording, keep the claim.

feature: fantasy prose as the language of dreams

verdict.trueWording: The best fantasy is written in the language of dreams.
verdict.note: Opening sentence of 'On Fantasy'. The rest of the claim is also carried: "We read fantasy to find the colors again... To taste strong spices", against "Reality is plywood and plastic, done up in mud brown and olive drab."

claim: The essay opposes fantasy's rich colors and spices to the drab strip-mall real, implying a prose that reaches for vivid sensory nouns.
quote: silver and scarlet, indigo and azure

verdict.trueWording: Fantasy is silver and scarlet, indigo and azure, obsidian veined with gold and lapis lazuli.
verdict.note: Quote is verbatim. The colors/spices-vs-drab-real opposition is explicit, including the strip mall: "Reality is the strip malls of Burbank, the smokestacks of Cleveland, a parking garage in Newark." The trailing gloss 'implying a prose that reaches for vivid sensory nouns' is the claimant's inference about prose technique, not something the essay states.

claim: Martin intentionally repeats phrases such as 'A Lannister always pays his debts' and remembered lines, a technique he says he took from Stephen King.
quote: I have learned this technique from Stephen King

verdict.trueWording: I have learned this technique from Stephen King and I like it very much.
verdict.note: Fully supported end to end. Martin: "There are certain sentences, like 'A Lannister always pays his debts'... I do it intentionally. I also like that Jaime remembers every day the sentence Tyrion said to him about Cersei." Page metadata confirms the cited date (October 8 2012).

claim: Martin handles magic like salt in a stew, a little improving it and too much ruining it; elsewhere he says explicit magic ceases to be magical.
quote: like a little salt in a stew

verdict.trueWording: It's like a little salt in a stew, I think.
verdict.note: Quote verbatim, and the mechanism is stated: "You put in a little salt, the stew tastes a lot better. You put in too much salt and ruin the stew." Caveat: the claim's second half ('elsewhere he says explicit magic ceases to be magical') is NOT on this page — searches for 'ceases to be magic' and 'explicit' returned nothing. The claim flags it as 'elsewhere', so it is uncited rather than miscited, but it currently rests on no source and needs one. Byline confirmed: Amy Gentry, LoneStarCon 3.

feature: thematic core: the heart in conflict
claim: Martin quotes Faulkner that the only thing worth writing about is the human heart in conflict with itself, which drives his interior POV.

verdict.trueWording: The only thing worth writing about is the human heart in conflict with itself.
verdict.note: Verbatim, and Martin explicitly frames it as his credo: "My credo as a writer has always been Faulkner's Nobel Prize acceptance speech where he said..." One overreach: 'which drives his interior POV' is the claimant's inference — on this page Martin invokes Faulkner to argue that magic must never be the solution to the problem, not to explain viewpoint.

claim: Martin cites the Iliad as a model where the hero of one side is the villain of the other, shaping his multi-sided viewpoint scheme.

verdict.trueWording: date from 1451, 1488, and 1400 respectively
